newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels "playing games" with refugee lives.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels "playing games" with refugee lives.

text.p: Aid workers on Sunday accused Zairean rebels of playing games with the lives of Rwandan refugees and warned many faced death because of delays in their repatriation.

"The situation at the moment is completely unacceptable," one aid worker told Reuters. "We need to put pressure on the (rebel) Alliance, on governments, on whoever it takes to get those people out of there."

Around 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees have been living in appalling conditions at Biaro and Kasese camps south of Kisangani since rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo/Zaire captured the city on March 15.
The death toll from cholera, malaria and malnutrition stands at around 40 a day with bodies lined up under blankets along a mud road leading through the camps.
Rebel leaders have given the go-ahead to a United Nations repatriation plan, but on Friday the U.N. refugee agency was forced to postpone it indefinitely after protests from regional authorities.
The authorities said a cholera outbreak at Kasese camp could spread to local residents if refugees were transferred by truck to the airport for repatriation.
The UNHCR has dismissed their fears as groundless and an official from the U.S.-based Centre for Disease Control flew to Kisangani on Saturday to add weight to the argument.
"At the moment they (the authorities) are just playing games with peoples' lives," another aid worker said.
Twenty-three new cholera cases were reported on Friday, bringing the total to 408 since mid-March. Some 42 people have died from the disease, according to UNHCR figures.
Angry locals broke the windscreen of a U.N. vehicle returning from the camps on Saturday on the second day of protests against the refugees and the presence of aid workers.
Privately aid officials say they fear the protests may be orchestrated by the Alliance to dress-up a shift in policy over repatriation.

They say this could be either because Rwanda is becoming overwhelmed after months of refugees returning and is putting pressure on the Alliance to halt the repatriation, or it could indicate a split between rebel leaders and local authorities.
"There seems to be a conscious effort to delay any move towards repatriation and this is putting people's lives at risk," an aid worker said.
"We were talking about going forward, but on two successive days humanitarian workers and assistance going to the camps have been attacked," another said.
"This is not a question of how we are going to repatriate people. This is not about an airlift. This is an effort to stop us going to the camps."
There was no immediate comment from the rebels on the accusations.
Conditions for the refugees have been made worse by torrential rains which have turned the Kisangani camps to mud.
Channels of dirty water run between tents set up on a steep slope by a stream while refugees, many painfully thin, look for shelter.

"I saw a woman standing in the rain holding a baby. She had no sheeting to cover her," said Antoinette Tshefu, head of the Zairean aid agency Omnis. "In another tent there were three children with no food, nothing. Their mother was in hospital."
"I have seen these refugees before but never in such desperate condition. Whatever has happened in the past these children and women should not pay for what others have done," she added said.

More than one million Hutu refugees fled East Zaire camps last October and November at the start of the campaign by rebels who control more than half of the vast country and are advancing on the capital Kinshasa.

Most refugees returned home in November but hundreds of thousands fled west including members of the former Rwandan army and the militia held responsible for massacres during the 1994 Rwanda genocide.
